data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a pragmatic, non-inductive rule of action based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness), where scientists choose the theory that has survived the severest tests because it is currently the closest approximation to truth, not because it is probable.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the definition of verisimilitude relies on inductive assumptions about the stability of laws.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory necessarily implies a belief in its future success, which is an inductive leap.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between 'probability' (logical likelihood) and 'verisimilitude' (closeness to truth). A theory with high empirical content that survives severe testing has high verisimilitude. The scientist's preference is a rational choice to act on the best available approximation of truth to solve problems, without assuming the future will resemble the past (induction).","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
